checks.claim: Stem: sunlight passes through the air and warms the ground; the warm ground gives off infrared toward space; water vapour, CO2 and a few other gases keep the ground warmer
Key: greenhouse gases absorb the rays and send part of them back down
Wrong choice: they reflect the rays back down like a mirror (absorption and re-emission, not reflection; a common misconception)
Wrong choice: they trap all the rays so none escape (outgoing longwave about 240 W/m2 balances absorbed sunlight)
Wrong choice: they stop warm air rising as a glass roof does (that is how a glass greenhouse mostly works; the atmospheric effect is radiative)
Context: energy given off again in any direction, part down and part up (about half downward on average)
Context: Earth sends about as much energy to space as it takes in from sunlight
Context: a glass greenhouse works mostly by keeping its warm air from rising and drifting off
Framing: settled physics only, no forecast, policy or alarm
Stem: nitrogen and oxygen are about 99 percent of dry air (78 + 21)
Stem: ground infrared passes through N2 and O2 almost untouched (only a very minor collision-induced absorption)

Key: their molecules are pairs of identical atoms (homonuclear diatomic). Wikipedia gives exactly this as the reason: two atoms of the same element, so no asymmetry of charge; the context supplies the physical reason (no changing dipole when the pair vibrates). It also sets them apart from H2O, CO2 and CH4, which all have three or more atoms
Wrong choice: lighter than water's or methane's (false: N2 28 and O2 32 g/mol are heavier than H2O 18 and CH4 16)
Wrong choice: too unreactive to take in any energy (false: oxygen is highly reactive, and both gases take up heat by collision)
Wrong choice: colourless, so the rays pass (false as the distinguishing reason: CO2, methane and water vapour are colourless too)
Context: when the pair vibrates its charge stays evenly spread, so it cannot catch infrared (the correct physical reason: no change of dipole moment during vibration)

Context: molecules of three or more atoms such as H2O, CO2 and CH4 bend and stretch lopsidedly and so absorb (CO2's bend and asymmetric stretch change its dipole; all gases of three or more atoms are infrared active)
Context: water and methane lighter than nitrogen; all colourless; oxygen highly reactive
Stem: Eunice Foote, 1856, two matching glass cylinders with thermometers inside (two in each), set in sunshine; one CO2, one common air
Stem: read the thermometers every few minutes (every two to three minutes), then took the cylinders out of the sun
Key: the CO2 grew hotter and stayed hot longer ('very sensibly more so than the other'; 'many times as long in cooling')
Wrong choices: ordinary air hotter; equal; CO2 hotter but cooled faster (all contradicted by her paper)

Context: CO2 reached 125 F against 106 F for ordinary air 'in her tests' (Grokipedia's table of her maxima in sunlight: hydrogen 104, common air 106, oxygen 108, carbonic acid gas 125; the hedge 'in her tests' covers that these are her maxima, not one paired run)
Context: took many times as long to cool; she wrote that an atmosphere of that gas would give Earth a high temperature (paraphrase, not in quotation marks)
Context: Joseph Henry read her paper at the AAAS meeting in Albany, New York, that August (23 August 1856)
Context: her cylinders took in the whole of sunlight and could not single out the ground's infrared; Tyndall did that three years later (1859)
Stem: Tyndall began measuring gas absorption at the Royal Institution in London in 1859 (apparatus set up there 9 May 1859)
Stem: rays from a copper cube of boiling water (lampblacked face) down a long brass tube (4 feet, rock-salt ends) to a detector (thermopile) at the far end
Stem: nitrogen and oxygen let almost all the heat pass (about 1 degree of deflection each); laboratory air absorbed far more (15)

Key: water vapour did most of the absorbing (Tyndall: aqueous vapour 'at least equal to thirteen times that of the atmosphere itself'; Wikipedia: he concluded water vapour is the strongest absorber of radiant heat in the atmosphere)
Wrong choice: carbon dioxide (absorbed too, but far less of the laboratory air's total, there being far less of it)
Wrong choices: methane and ozone (both tested by Tyndall as gases, but only traces in laboratory air)
Context: water vapour at least thirteen times the dry air; strongest absorber among the air's gases; CO2 absorbed too but is far scarcer
Context: he wrote that every change in the air's water vapour must change the climate (paraphrase of 'every variation of this constituent must produce a change of climate', 1861 paper)
Stem: Arrhenius, Swedish chemist (physicist and chemist), thousands of manual calculations, published 1896

Stem: used Samuel Langley's measurements of infrared from the Moon (taken through different thicknesses of air) to get the absorption of CO2 and water vapour (Wikipedia: observations by Langley and his assistant Frank Washington Very at the Allegheny Observatory; 'Langley's measurements' is the usual short form)
Stem: computed the change for each band of latitude with less or more CO2 (K = 0.67, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, by 10-degree zones)
Key: the puzzle was what brought on the ice ages ('no satisfactory hypothesis that could explain how the climatic conditions for an ice age' could arise; AIP: drawn to the riddle of the ice ages)
Wrong choices: cities warmer than countryside; Venus hotter than Earth; poles colder than tropics (none was his motive)
Context: CO2 cut to 0.62-0.55 (a little over half) would cool the 40th-50th parallels by 4-5 C, enough for an ice age
Context: doubling would warm Earth by about 5 to 6 degrees (Table VII, K=2: 4.95 to 6.05 C by latitude; AIP and Grokipedia 5-6 C)
checks.note: True as history, but it is a climate-sensitivity figure (how much a doubling of CO2 warms Earth): the facts sheet itself leaves sensitivity to the T5 unit, and the figure is about twice today's central estimate, so a child may take 5-6 degrees as the present answer. It strays toward the 'how much warming' ground the framing rules out. Fix: drop the clause, e.g. 'Arrhenius calculated that cutting the air's carbon dioxide to a little over half would cool the middle latitudes by 4 to 5 degrees Celsius, enough, he thought, for an ice age.' ('calculated ... he thought' also keeps his ice-age cause as his hypothesis, since ice ages are now paced by Earth's orbit with CO2 as an amplifier.)

checks.claim: Context: he called the work tedious calculations ('I should certainly not have undertaken these tedious calculations')
Stem: many 1950s scientists expected the oceans to absorb nearly all the CO2 from fuel burning
Stem: Keeling began measuring at Mauna Loa in March 1958 (29 March), observatory at about 3,400 m on bare lava, remote from continents

Key: by 1960 his readings showed the gas building up year after year (Scripps: 'In 1959 the average concentration had increased and increased still further in 1960'; his 1960 Tellus paper reported the rise, which AIP notes rested partly on his Antarctic record)
Wrong choices: holding steady soaked up by oceans; slowly falling; jumping with no clear pattern (he found a clear seasonal cycle plus a rise)
Context: first reading 313 ppm
Context: the yearly average has risen every year since (NOAA Mauna Loa growth rates 1959-2025 all positive; lowest 0.31 in 1964)
Context: about 430 ppm by early 2026 (NOAA monthly means: Jan 428.62, Feb 429.35, Mar 430.15). Changes over time; the question does not rest on it
Context: yearly rise grew from about 0.7 to more than 2.5 ppm (NOAA: 1959-1964 average 0.68; 1960s decade 0.86; 2020-2025 average 2.56)
Context: Revelle and Suess had already shown (1957) that surface sea water takes up far less CO2 than a simple calculation predicts ('barely one-tenth')
Framing: measured record only, no forecast or attribution of warming

Stem: readings fall from about May until October, then climb to the next May (Grokipedia: September-October minimum, May maximum; NOAA monthly minimum falls in September in most recent years, October in others; Keeling's 1958 minimum was October)
Stem: a swing of about six ppm (Grokipedia about 6 ppm; NOAA 2025 May 430.51 to Sep 424.37, 6.1 ppm)
Key: northern forests and fields growing, then dying back (Northern Hemisphere land plants take CO2 in spring and summer; decay returns it in autumn and winter)
Wrong choice: southern forests and fields (their seasons are opposite and the south has far less land; the cycle tracks the northern seasons)
Wrong choices: polar sea ice freezing and melting; the volcano venting more and less (neither drives the cycle; volcanic plumes are screened out of the record)
Context: most land, and so most plants, in the northern half ('Most of this vegetation is in the Northern Hemisphere, where most of the land is located')
Context: northern plants take CO2 in spring and summer; dead leaves and plants decay and give it back in autumn and winter
Context: the South Pole record shows almost no yearly swing (Grokipedia: 'minimal seasonal variability'; about 1 ppm against about 6 at Mauna Loa)
Key: leaving aside limestone and rocks like it, the oceans hold the most (about 38,000 GtC, 'the largest active carbon reservoir')
Stem qualifier: 'limestone and other rocks like it' sets aside the carbonate rocks only
checks.note: Limestone-like (carbonate) rocks hold 60-65 million GtC, but kerogen, the organic carbon in shale and other sedimentary rocks, holds another 15 million GtC and the upper mantle on the order of 120 million GtC; neither is 'like' limestone, so read literally the stem's qualifier leaves stores far larger than the ocean in play. The key is still the only right choice of the four. Fix: set aside all rocks, e.g. 'Leaving aside the vast amount locked up in rocks such as limestone, which store holds the most carbon?'

checks.claim: Wrong choice: living things and the soil (vegetation 450-650 GtC, soil 1,500-2,400, permafrost 1,460-1,600: at most about 4,700, far below the ocean)
Wrong choice: fossil fuels such as coal and oil (about 5,000-10,000 GtC)
Wrong choice: the air (about 800-900 GtC)
Context: sea water about 38,000 billion tonnes, forty to fifty times the air (38,000 / 900 = 42; / 800 = 48; WHOI about 50 times)
Context: coal, oil and gas perhaps 5,000-10,000; soil 1,500-2,400; living plants 450-650 billion tonnes
Context: plants take carbon from the air, breathing and decay return it, the sea dissolves it, burning returns fossil carbon buried for millions of years
Stem: Tambora, on Sumbawa, Indonesia, exploded in April 1815 (climax 10 April); the largest eruption in recorded history ('the largest and most powerful volcanic explosion in recorded history')
Stem: cloud rose more than 40 km, into the stratosphere (up to 43 km)
Stem: next year (1816) snow in New England in June (up to six inches on 6 June) and crops failed across Europe
Key: tiny droplets formed from its sulfur gas (SO2 oxidised to sulfate aerosols that reflect sunlight)
Wrong choice: fine ash (removed within several days to weeks; little impact on climate)
Wrong choices: steam and carbon dioxide (greenhouse gases; Tambora's CO2 negligible)
Context: about 60 million tonnes of SO2 into the stratosphere (Grokipedia: 53-58 Tg in one section, about 60 megatons in others)
Context: sulfuric acid droplets reflected sunlight for a year or more; 1816 the year without a summer (aerosols 1-3 years; effects to 1818)
Context: ash falls out within days to weeks; steam and CO2 warm rather than cool

unit_notes: No hard errors. Two items flagged uncertain: the Arrhenius context's doubling figure (true as history, but a climate-sensitivity number the unit's framing leaves out) and the carbon-stores stem's 'rocks like it' (kerogen in shale and the mantle are not like limestone yet hold far more than the ocean). Optional polish, not errors: (1) Q1 context 'A greenhouse gas molecule absorbs an infrared ray and soon gives the energy off again': in the lower air the absorbing molecule nearly always hands the energy to its neighbours by collision first, and the warmed air then gives off infrared of its own in every direction; 'The gases absorb the rays, and the warmed air gives off infrared of its own in every direction' is as simple and exact. The key's 'absorb and send part back down' is the standard simplification and stands. (2) Q7 stem 'from about May until October': NOAA's monthly minimum falls in September in most recent years (Grokipedia: a September-October minimum); 'until late September or October' would be exact. (3) Q2: the key 'pairs of identical atoms' is right, as Wikipedia gives it; the context correctly adds the physical reason (no change of charge balance when the pair vibrates). Framing elsewhere is clean: no forecast, policy, attribution of warming or alarm.
